nameStory: The 'floating' part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive habit of growing partially submerged in water, with its long leaves and stems often floating on the surface. The 'bur-reed' name refers to the spiky, round seed heads that look like tiny medieval maces or burrs, while the long narrow leaves resemble those of cattails and other reedy wetland plants.
description: Floating bur-reed is an aquatic perennial plant that grows in shallow water and wetlands throughout New England, though it's quite rare and endangered in Connecticut. It produces long, ribbon-like leaves that can float on the water's surface and distinctive round, spiky flower and seed clusters arranged along branching stems. The plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall, with much of its length often trailing in the water, creating an almost grass-like underwater meadow effect in suitable habitats.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, round clusters arranged like beads on a string along the stem - upper clusters are male (releasing yellow pollen), lower ones are female (green and spiky like tiny hedgehogs)

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves that feel smooth and somewhat rubbery, often floating on water surface or trailing underwater

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows partially submerged in shallow water, with flowering stems emerging above surface while much of the plant trails below

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Spiky, burr-like seed heads that feel rough and prickly to the touch, turning brown as they mature in late summer

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, somewhat triangular stems in cross-section that feel firm but flexible, often with a zigzag branching pattern

habitat: Found in shallow ponds, slow-moving streams, marshes, and the edges of lakes with soft, muddy bottoms. Prefers acidic to neutral water and can tolerate seasonal water level changes. Often grows alongside other aquatic plants like pondweeds, water lilies, and other bur-reed species in quiet backwaters and protected coves.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from underwater rootstocks as water warms, appearing as bright green ribbons just below the surface.
seasonality.summer: Flowering stems rise above water in mid to late summer, displaying the characteristic round flower clusters that make identification easiest.
seasonality.fall: Spiky seed heads mature and turn brown, while leaves may begin to yellow and die back as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, leaving only underwater rootstocks and sometimes persistent dried seed heads poking through ice.

funFact: Floating bur-reed is so rare in Connecticut that it's listed as endangered there, with only a handful of known populations - making any sighting a genuine botanical treasure hunt discovery worth reporting to local naturalists!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bur-reed species, but floating bur-reed's preference for deeper water and its more delicate, truly floating leaves help distinguish it. The round, spiky flower/seed clusters immediately separate it from cattails, which have the familiar brown 'hot dog' shaped flower spikes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bur-reed,' this plant isn't closely related to true reeds but belongs to the same family as cattails. The spiky seed heads were sometimes used by Native Americans for various purposes, though this species was likely too uncommon to be regularly harvested.
compareHints: Floating bur-reed differs from its relatives by truly living up to its name - it floats more readily than American or big bur-reed, which tend to grow in shallower water with more erect stems. Its leaves are typically more delicate and ribbon-like compared to the broader, more robust leaves of big bur-reed, and it generally grows in deeper water than the small, often terrestrial unbranched bur-reed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American bur-reed can be distinguished from its bur-reed relatives primarily by size and habitat - it's mid-sized compared to the massive big bur-reed or the tiny small bur-reed.
Big bur-reed stands out from other bur-reeds by being the largest and having the biggest, most impressive spiky seed heads - it's truly the giant of the group.
Among New England's bur-reeds, this species has the narrowest leaves and is the most aquatic, rarely growing in anything but deep water.
Among New England's bur-reeds, unbranched bur-reed is distinguished by its single, straight flowering stem and relatively wide leaves with keeled bases.
Small bur-reed is much more delicate and usually stays submerged compared to its relatives like American bur-reed or big bur-reed, which stand tall above water like cattails.
Branching bur-reed is distinguished from other bur-reeds primarily by its branching flower arrangement - most other species like unbranched bur-reed keep their spiky balls in a simple single row.
